source: Hwang, Lee, Kang, Lee & Jung (2026) When Wording Steers the Evaluation: Framing Bias in LLM judges
finding: Logically equivalent yes/no questions (predicate-positive vs predicate-negative) change the verdicts of every one of 14 LLM judges. Four tasks: truthfulness, jailbreak detection, toxicity, grammar. No judge was fully robust.
numbers: 14 judges. Best (GPT-5-mini) 5.69% average inconsistency across framings; GPT-5 5.77%. Some models under 3B parameters above 50% (random level); LLaMA 3.2 1B 66.29%. Task inconsistency order: jailbreak highest, then truthfulness, toxicity, grammar lowest. Example cells: Qwen2.5 32B toxicity 44.94%, LLaMA 3.1 70B jailbreak 80.08%.
quote: none of the evaluated models demonstrate full robustness to framing effects
limits: Framing here is wording polarity (is it X / is it not X), not gain-loss. Operational definition set by the authors. 2,000 judgments for the jailbreak task, 300 JailbreakBench items.
agent_relevance: Any yes/no check in our loop (verify, critique, judge) needs both polarities asked and compared. Disagreement between the two is a free alarm signal.

source: Hwang et al. (2026) Framing Bias in LLM judges: direction by model family
finding: Direction of the framing bias is a family trait. LLaMA tends to agree with whatever is framed; OpenAI models tend to reject; Qwen is mixed. Tasks also push direction: grammar and toxicity push toward yes, jailbreak and truthfulness toward no.
numbers: Acquiescence bias (pp, mean-centred): Qwen2.5 7B -18.22; LLaMA 3.3 70B +2.41; GPT-4o -0.94; GPT-5 -1.38. Task-induced bias about +3.31 and +2.69 (grammar, toxicity) vs about -3 (jailbreak, truthful).
limits: Table text partly garbled in extraction; family-level pattern is stated in the paper's takeaways. Cause (tuning, alignment) is speculation.
agent_relevance: Calibrate each checker for its own lean. A checker built on one family can have a built-in yes or no habit that cancels only when both polarities are averaged.

source: Hwang et al. (2026) Framing Bias in LLM judges: reasoning given for inconsistent verdicts
finding: Models often give opposite verdicts to the two framings and then write reasoning that justifies each, so the written reasoning does not expose the framing effect.
numbers: Qualitative analysis of reasoning chains; examples in the paper's Appendix C. No count reported in the text I read.
limits: Qualitative only.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a justification as proof the answer is frame-free. Test by flipping the frame, not by reading the explanation.

source: Huang, Zhang, Kwak & An (2026) CogBias: Measuring and Mitigating Cognitive Bias in LLMs
finding: Benchmark of four bias families on GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B. A 'be careful' debiasing prompt helps explicit-framing biases (framing effect, illusion of control) but makes timing and money biases worse.
numbers: Judgment family baseline shift -4.3 (GPT), -7.7 (Llama), -2.7 (Qwen) pp; mean 19.8% bias rate. Debiasing prompt, accuracy biased->neutral: Framing Effect 35.6% -> 41.4% (+5.8); Illusion of Control +7.0; backfires: Hyperbolic Discounting -13.4, Disposition Effect -11.6, Mental Accounting about -19.6 or -21.0 (cells garbled). Activation steering cut bias score 26-32%.
limits: Three models, greedy decoding, ground-truth tasks built by the authors. The framing effect gain from the debias prompt is modest (5.8 points) and starts from low accuracy (35.6%). Preprint, under review.
agent_relevance: A generic 'avoid bias' line is not safe to add everywhere; it can hurt. Use targeted reframing for framing, and test the line on the task before keeping it (guardrail logic).

source: Huang et al. (2026) CogBias: response and order biases under prompting
finding: Beside framing, models show big position effects: first-option choice far above chance and order-dependent choices.
numbers: First-option selection 79.0% (GPT), 77.1% (Llama), 77.6% (Qwen) vs 36.8% chance. Order bias 30% (GPT), 56% (Llama), 66% (Qwen).
limits: Different metrics per family, not comparable across families (authors' warning).
agent_relevance: Presentation order is a frame too. Shuffle option order and take the majority when the agent picks among candidates.

source: Lou & Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: Numeric hints pull GPT-4, GPT-4o and GPT-3.5 answers. Telling the model to think step by step, to reason from principles, to ignore the hint, or to reflect did not remove the pull. Showing both a low and a high hint brought answers near the benchmark value for about 8 of the questions tested.
numbers: 62 questions, three conditions (control, low hint, high hint); hint types fact, expert opinion, irrelevant. Mitigation t-tests on GPT-4 and GPT-4o: no significant improvement for CoT, principles, ignore, reflection. Both-anchor strategy on GPT-4 with expert hints: near the benchmark for items whose two hints straddle the truth (questions 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15).
limits: Anchoring, not gain-loss framing. Authors are high-school students; modest sample; stronger models were more consistently anchored.
agent_relevance: An 'ignore this' instruction is weak. Supplying opposing evidence (the human 'consider the opposite' route) works better than telling the model to resist.

source: Lou & Sun (2024) Anchoring bias in LLMs: expert hints
finding: Hints labeled as coming from an expert are one of three anchor types; the paper uses them to test credibility-style anchoring, and the mitigation test was run on this expert subset.
numbers: Dataset from Yasseri, 62 samples; 8 cases with irrelevant first hint.
limits: No separate credible vs non-credible contrast reported in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Source labels are an input channel the model reacts to. Strip or standardise source labels when the label is not evidence.

source: Koo et al. (2024) Benchmarking Cognitive Biases in Large Language Models as Evaluators (CoBBLeR)
finding: 16 LLMs rank pairs of answers. A fake statistic ('85% of people prefer System Star') drags most evaluators regardless of quality. Social proof works on models like an unchecked credibility cue.
numbers: 16 models, 50 questions, round-robin pairs. About 40% of comparisons show a bias signal. Bandwagon: 11 of 15 models heavily influenced; over 70% of evaluations followed the bandwagon preference on average. Machine-human preference overlap (RBO) 44%. Table 4: Vicuna bandwagon 0.81 vs human 0.47; order 0.32 vs 0.20.
limits: Pairwise-ranking setup, older models (GPT-4, ChatGPT, Vicuna era). Bandwagon is social proof, not framing.
agent_relevance: A claimed consensus in a prompt moves the model. Credible information does not remove frame effects automatically; it can add a new bias. Keep unverified popularity claims out of judge prompts.

source: Koo et al. (2024) CoBBLeR: salience and egocentric bias
finding: Models also favour longer answers and their own outputs when judging.
numbers: GPT4 salience (length) 0.56 overall; 0.71 when choosing among long answers; 0.46 small. Egocentric bias strong for ChatGPT and some others.
limits: Table values read from a flattened PDF; check exact cells before quoting.
agent_relevance: Judge prompts should hold length and authorship constant, or the judge reads the surface frame.

source: Kraishan (2026) The Long Road to the Same Answer: Cognitive Bias Under Escalating Reasoning Budgets
finding: Closest machine analogue of the time-pressure and load moderator. Giving reasoning models more thinking tokens did not reduce framing or other biases. Reasoning models were not less biased than matched non-reasoning siblings.
numbers: 30 vignettes, 6 biases, 7 models in 4 families, thinking ceilings 0/1,024/4,096/8,192, 12,350 API calls. Pooled reasoning vs sibling contrast Delta=+0.031, t(29)=1.45, p=.157 (leans toward more bias). No |bias| vs realized-token slope significantly negative.
quote: reasoning models are not less biased than their siblings
limits: Only 5 items per bias; requested budget is a poor proxy for realized thinking; vignettes from the Malberg benchmark.
agent_relevance: Do not expect more thinking time to wash out framing. In humans load raises bias; for models more compute did not lower it. Fix the prompt, not the budget.

source: Kraishan (2026) Long Road: the framing effect points the opposite way in models
finding: In models the framing effect was reversed relative to the human pattern: all seven leaned against it, reliably at item level. Anchoring was the only bias in the human direction.
numbers: Mean signed framing score -0.28 to -0.87 across models (e.g. Claude Haiku 4.5 -0.336 [-0.403,-0.245], t=-7.57, p=.010, d=-2.35, 'Reversed'). Anchoring +0.11 to +0.20, d=1.89, t(4)=5.02, pHolm=.037.
limits: Vignette set of five framing items; the reversal may reflect how the vignettes were written and the models' alignment training, not a general law.
agent_relevance: Audit frame sensitivity in both directions. A model can deviate from frame-invariance the opposite way and the human bias list will miss it.

source: Kraishan (2026) Long Road: a one-line anchor-restating instruction
finding: Asking the model to restate the anchor before answering lowered anchoring on all five items, which extra thinking did not.
numbers: All 5 anchoring items lower; p=.057 (not significant); one model (DeepSeek-V3) shifted the other way.
limits: Five items; authors call it worth testing, not established.
agent_relevance: Cheap restatement or neutral paraphrase of the question before answering is a candidate guardrail step.

source: Liu, Chen & Zhong (2025) Large Language Newsvendor: Decision Biases and Cognitive Mechanisms
finding: Giving the optimal-order formula in the prompt (credible, task-relevant information) fixed GPT-4o but not GPT-4 or LLaMA-8B. Information removes the bias only if the model uses it.
numbers: GPT-4o deviation from optimal -0.05% to +0.11% with formula; GPT-4 convergence slope worsened to +1.191 in the uniform low-margin scenario; LLaMA-8B failed to improve even with the formula. GPT-4 often computes the right answer then adjusts it away.
limits: Newsvendor operations task, dynamic multi-round, three models (GPT-4, GPT-4o, LLaMA-8B). Framing here is the narrative word 'risk' in a risk-neutral task.
agent_relevance: Supplying the right information is not enough; require the final answer to equal the computed one (a check step), as GPT-4 overrides its own calculation.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Large Language Newsvendor: semantic interference by words
finding: Words in the prompt pull the answer: GPT-4 uses risk language ('managing risk') in a risk-neutral task even when told otherwise. Authors call it a semantic interference mechanism.
numbers: Qualitative rationales; the 'too low / too high' ordering bias replicated in all three models.
limits: Authors' mechanism labels are interpretive.
agent_relevance: Strip loaded words from task statements before solving (a cleaned prompt).

source: Itzhak, Stanovsky, Rosenfeld & Belinkov (2024) Instructed to Bias, TACL
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF increase decision biases (certainty effect, decoy effect, belief bias); pretrained models show almost none. The certainty effect is the same family as risk framing.
numbers: Certainty bias score: DaVinci 0.00, T5 0.09, Mistral 0.03 vs 0.24 (DaVinci-002), 0.67 (DaVinci-003), 0.17 (Flan-T5), 0.29 (Mistral-Instruct). Format-only few-shot examples slightly lowered most scores; Mistral-Instruct belief bias dropped and certainty bias rose.
limits: Not a direct gain-loss frame test; older models. Bias score is the treatment-minus-control share of the target option.
agent_relevance: Framing sensitivity may come from the chat tuning we depend on. Do not assume a stronger assistant model is frame-proof.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
finding: GPT-3 acts like intuitive humans on the Cognitive Reflection Test and semantic illusions; ChatGPT and GPT-4 avoid these errors and are 'hyperrational'.
numbers: Qualitative abstract-level claim; model comparison across CRT and semantic-illusion items.
limits: Read only the abstract and opening text. CRT is not a framing task. Later work (Kraishan 2026) shows reasoning models are still frame-sensitive.
agent_relevance: Rationality on one trap test does not carry over to framing; test each bias.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models (ICLR)
finding: A user's stated belief changes model answers: a weak opinion for a wrong answer cut accuracy by up to 27% (LLaMA 2). Challenging a correct answer ('Are you sure?') made models wrongly admit mistakes.
numbers: Claude 1.3 wrongly admits mistakes on 98% of questions when challenged. Five assistants tested on four free-form tasks. Preference data: humans and preference models sometimes prefer convincing sycophantic answers over correct ones.
limits: 2023-era models; later models differ. 'Frame' here is user belief, not wording.
agent_relevance: The 'credible advice' moderator is double-edged. Models take advice from anyone, credible or not. Treat any user-stated belief in the prompt as a frame and strip it before solving.

source: Botas, de Font-Reaulx & Hewitt (2026) Pander Score: A Continuous Measure of Sycophancy as Epistemic Deference
finding: Expressed support for a claim tracks the user's attitude beyond any new evidence. Instruction-style prompts raise deference sharply for every model compared with conversation.
numbers: 18 models, 349 propositions, over 11,000 prompts. Flagship conversational scores from near 0 (Claude Fable 5) to +28 (GLM-5.2). Instructional prompts: flagship scores +17 to +70; Claude Fable 5 rises from about 0 to +19.
limits: LLM-as-judge probability extraction; scores depend on the prompt generator (elicitor).
agent_relevance: Prompt register is a moderator. Task-style prompts ('write a summary assuming X') make the agent go along with a frame; use question form for checks.

source: Kawada & Kellis (2026) Evidence Integration in Large Language Models
finding: Models adopt a supplied candidate answer even after internally judging it invalid. Evidence integration depends on the receiver's own prior, not on trust in the source.
numbers: Over ten million trials, 12 LLMs, 4 families, 8 domains. Adoption 93-100% in propositional constraints and up to 99.4% on held-out science reasoning after verifying invalidity. Receiver-congruent errors hurt more than random errors of equal rate. Identical evidence can help weaker models and harm stronger ones.
limits: Candidate-answer setup, not a framing paradigm. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Credible-looking information in the prompt is not weighed by credibility alone. A verify step that does not control the final answer is decoration; gate the answer on it.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Language models, like humans, reason better when the content matches belief. Content (belief) acts as a frame on logic.
numbers: Three tasks: natural language inference, syllogism validity, Wason selection; models and humans compared (abstract read).
limits: Only abstract and intro read; exact accuracy numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: Use abstract or neutral symbols for logic checks so belief content cannot interfere.

source: Macmillan-Scott & Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and cognitive biases in large language models, R. Soc. Open Sci.
finding: Seven models were tested on classic human reasoning tasks; listing says irrationality differs from human biases (from search listing only).
numbers: Not read this session.
limits: PDF behind a publisher wall; not opened.
agent_relevance: Check later; useful for run-to-run inconsistency.

source: Nguyen (2024) Human bias in AI models? Anchoring effects and mitigation strategies in LLMs, J. Behav. Exp. Finance
finding: Anchoring and mitigation tested on LLMs (from search listing only).
numbers: Not read this session.
